 A 2024 Ford Maverick Lariat owner thought taking advantage of Ford's mobile service for safety recall 26C10 would save a trip to the dealer. Instead, he said a digital tracking glitch left his truck stuck in recall limbo after the repair was finished. 
 Advertising 
 November 3, 2026 - 5:07PM EST 
 By: Blake Lowry 
 Key Takeaways 
 The Fix Is Working: Ford's software patch for Recall 26C10 is active and successfully fixes the trailer brake and lighting drop-out bug.
 The Driveway Glitch: Mobile techs can flash your truck at home, but weak cellular connections can prevent Ford's database from marking the recall complete.
 Manual Dealer Flash Required: 2022–2024 Mavericks cannot get this safety patch over-the-air (OTA); they require a physical diagnostic cable plug-in.
 Ford’s promise of mobile driveway service is meant to take the hassle out of safety recalls. Instead of dropping off your truck at a dealership lot and losing half a day in a customer waiting lounge, a factory-trained technician comes directly to your home.
 For one 2024 Ford Maverick Lariat owner , scheduling Ford's mobile unit to clear compliance recall 26C10 (NHTSA Campaign 26V104 ) felt like modern truck ownership at its finest. The recall, which impacts roughly 412,000 Mavericks nationwide, addresses a safety-critical timing glitch in the Integrated Trailer Module (ITRM).
 He claims the technician arrived, plugged in diagnostic tools, and successfully flashed the new software right on the driveway. But when the tech attempted to close out the job, the experience took a frustrating turn into software limbo : the physical repair on the truck was finished, but Ford's corporate tracking servers refused to register the recall as complete.
 What Happened During the Driveway Recall Visit? 
 According to him, the driveway visit was arranged to avoid taking time out of his day:
 "I had a recall service yesterday with my dealer for the latest towing recall. I am sharing because there is something new happening and I thought you all should know about it... My dealer set a remote service call, where they were going to come to my home to fix the issue... My dealer has seen this happen several times in the last few weeks, and are submitting reports to Ford to correct and close these recalls."
 The technician hooked up a Ford VCM III diagnostic interface to the OBD-II port and successfully applied the updated calibration file using the Ford Diagnostic and Repair System (FDRS). The patch was designed to eliminate a startup communication timing glitch between the ITRM and the Body Control Module.
 Without the patch, the glitch can throw a "Trailer Brake Module Fault" or "Blind Spot Assist Unavailable" alert on the dash . While the Maverick’s own lights function normally, connected trailer brake lights, turn indicators, and electric trailer brakes disengage completely.
 However, when the technician attempted to officially close out the safety campaign in Ford’s central database, the system hit a wall. The owners said the recall remained flagged as active on the vehicle record, leaving the dealership unable to mark the safety ticket complete despite having physically serviced the truck.
 Is the Recall Fix Officially Available? 
 Yes, Ford has released the official software patch to resolve the safety defect. However, early in the rollout, dealers faced hurdles getting the update to stick on 2022–2024 model years, even as 2025 and 2026 trucks were being updated. As forum participant MavStangVa noted:
 "For a while, even my dealer could not do my 24 Lariat even though 25 and 26 vehicles were getting the patch. Ford finally figured out how to do the earlier models."
 While the calibration file is now fully working, the administrative close-out process remains the primary snag for driveway service calls.
 Why Cellular Latency Causes "Recall Limbo"
 This owner's experience sparked a wider community discussion regarding how Ford handles ECU module updates and warranty validation across different model years.
 Maverick Generation 
 How Recall 26C10 Is Applied 
 2022–2024 Models (Sync 3) 
 Requires physical FDRS cable flash via dealer bay or mobile tech 
 2025–2026 Models (Sync 4) 
 Supports full ECU module updates over the air or via FDRS 
 As another forum member clarified regarding model year capability:
 "MY22-24 with Sync 3 audio can get OTA updates only for the audio system and navigation updates. Only the MY25 and later can get OTA vehicle system updates/patches like the towing recall fix."
 Owners of 2022 through 2024 Mavericks run Ford’s legacy electrical architecture, which requires module-level recalibrations to be flashed manually using a wired FDRS connection. Unlike media or screen updates, critical safety modules like the trailer controller cannot update over the air on these earlier model years.
 Furthermore, when mobile technicians perform FDRS flashes in customer driveways using cellular hotspots, network latency or packet drops during the final PTS validation handshake can prevent Ford's central server from registering that the flash succeeded. The truck gets the updated software, but the corporate database still flags the VIN as non-compliant.
 What Should Maverick Owners Do Before Booking Service? 
 Verify the PTS Ticket with Your Service Advisor: Mobile tech visits can flash 2022–2024 Mavericks at home using FDRS tools, but always ask your service advisor to verify that the PTS warranty ticket was successfully marked complete in Ford's central system before the technician leaves.
 Use the 15-Minute Reset for False Alarms: If your dash pops a false "Trailer Brake Module Fault" message before you can get to the dealer, shut off the ignition, lock the doors, and let the truck rest for 15 minutes. This allows the high-speed CAN bus to enter deep sleep and reset the boot-up sequence.
 Request Printed Documentation: Always ask for a hard copy or digital receipt of the closed Repair Order (RO) showing the cleared campaign code to protect your vehicle's resale value and warranty history.
 Torque News Take: The Growing Pains of Software-Defined Trucks 
 The owner's claim of the driveway recall experience points to a larger structural challenge facing the auto industry as vehicles become increasingly dependent on interconnected digital architecture. Modern pickups are no longer just mechanical tools; they are rolling computer networks where physical wrenching has been replaced by cloud-based handshakes and diagnostic validation protocols.
 Mobile service programs are a major leap forward for customer convenience, but they rely heavily on seamless wireless execution behind the scenes. When a mobile technician's diagnostic laptop cannot cleanly validate a repair back to corporate servers over a cellular hotspot, the convenience of home service breaks down.
 For Maverick owners: the physical fix for Recall 26C10 is available and effective, but verifying that your truck's digital paper trail is officially cleared is just as important as getting the software installed. Until automakers bridge the gap between dealership diagnostic bays and cloud database tracking, staying proactive with your local service advisor remains your best defense against lingering recall alerts.
 Over to You: Have you experienced delays or app glitches while trying to get Recall 26C10 cleared on your Ford Maverick or F-150? Have you tried Ford's mobile service, or did you drop off your truck at the dealership? Let us know in the comments below!
